platforms.title: Itchy Skin After Swimming? 4 Fixes That Beat Chlorine Rash
platforms.meta_description: Tight, itchy skin after the pool is usually irritant contact dermatitis, not a chlorine allergy. What CDC and NHS guidance say to do in the hour after you swim.
platforms.body_html:
You spent the afternoon at the pool, and by evening the skin on your shoulders and forearms feels tight, hot and itchy — the kind of itch that gets worse the moment you notice it. Almost everyone assumes this is "a chlorine allergy." It usually is not. What happens to skin in a chlorinated pool has a specific name, a specific mechanism, and a fix that takes about four minutes if you do it in the right order. Here is what actually goes wrong, and the four things worth changing.

Chlorine Wrecks Your Skin Barrier — It Rarely Makes You Allergic

The NHS splits contact dermatitis into two mechanisms that get confused constantly. An irritant is a substance that directly damages the outer layer of skin. An allergen is a substance that makes the immune system respond in a way that affects the skin. The NHS is explicit that contact dermatitis is most commonly caused by irritants — soaps and detergents, solvents, and regular contact with water — while allergic contact dermatitis is the less common form.

Pool water sits squarely in the first category. DermNet describes irritant contact dermatitis as what happens when a chemical or physical agent damages the skin surface faster than the skin can repair it: irritants strip oils and natural moisturising factor out of the outer layer, which then lets more irritant through. The scale of this is easy to underrate — DermNet notes that occupational hand dermatitis is caused by irritants in 80 percent of cases, not by allergy.

The distinction is not academic, because it decides what test is worth doing. Patch testing — small amounts of known allergens taped to the back and read over several days — answers the allergy question. It does not diagnose irritant damage. If your skin only reacts after long pool sessions and calms down over the following week, you are looking at a barrier problem, and the useful moves are about exposure and repair rather than allergen hunting.

The Smell You Blame on Chlorine Is Mostly Chloramine

Here is the part that reframes the whole problem. CDC explains that chloramines form when chlorine combines with nitrogen-containing material that swimmers bring in — pee, poop, sweat and dirt. Chloramines are what irritate skin, eyes and the respiratory tract, and they are what produces the sharp "pool smell" people read as a sign of a well-chlorinated pool. Most health departments cap combined chlorine in the water at 0.4 ppm or less, precisely because that fraction is the irritating one.

Free chlorine itself is held at a level most people would find surprisingly low. CDC recommends pH 7.0 to 7.8 and a free chlorine concentration of at least 1 ppm in pools and at least 3 ppm in hot tubs, or at least 2 ppm in pools where cyanuric acid is used as a stabiliser. A properly run pool is not a chemical bath. It is a body of water whose irritant load rises with how many people got in without rinsing first.

That also explains why home pools deserve more caution than public ones. A CDC analysis in MMWR estimated 13,508 US emergency department visits for pool chemical injuries over 2015 to 2017, at least 56 percent of them at a residence and two thirds of them between Memorial Day weekend and Labor Day. Those are handling and storage injuries, not swimming ones — but they are a good reminder that concentrated pool chemicals are not household products.

Rinse Going In, Rinse Coming Out, Moisturise While Damp

Four changes, in the order they matter:

  • Take a rinse shower before you get in. CDC's reasoning is that even a quick rinse removes much of the body waste that forms chloramines in the first place — so a pre-swim rinse protects the water, and the water then irritates you less. Skip the folk version where you rinse half an hour ahead; the point is to arrive wet and clean, not to pre-soak on a timer.
  • Rinse off as soon as you get out. NHS prevention advice for contact dermatitis is to rinse skin that has met an irritant with warm water as soon as possible. On a long waterpark day, that means a rinse at the lunch break too, not just at closing time.
  • Swap the shower gel for an emollient wash. The NHS specifically suggests emollient soap substitutes rather than regular bar or liquid soaps, which dry the skin out — a detail most post-swim routines miss while adding a scented body wash on top of an already stripped barrier.
  • Moisturise while the skin is still damp. The NHS instruction is to gently dry after a bath or shower and then immediately apply the emollient while the skin is still moist, in a large amount, smoothed in the direction hair grows rather than rubbed. For very dry skin, two to four times a day. Ointments hold moisture best; creams and lotions sit better on inflamed areas.

What a Hydrocortisone Cream Can and Cannot Do

If the skin is genuinely inflamed and not just dry, a mild topical steroid is reasonable — with limits that are printed on the box and routinely ignored. In the UK, most hydrocortisone creams and ointments sold in shops and pharmacies are classed as mild steroids, and the NHS instruction is blunt: do not use hydrocortisone on your skin for more than 7 days unless a pharmacist or doctor tells you to. Do not use it on the face, penis or vulva without asking a pharmacist or doctor first, because it can damage the skin in those areas. Most adults and children aged 10 and over can use it; under-10s only on advice.

Two application details do most of the work. Apply a thin layer, once or twice a day — a fingertip unit covers an area twice the size of your palm. And if you are also using an emollient, the NHS advises applying the emollient first and waiting around 30 minutes before the steroid, so you are not diluting it across skin that has just been oiled. Hydrocortisone is also the wrong choice on broken skin, cold sores, chickenpox or shingles, or a bacterial skin infection.

Stop self-treating and get seen if the rash covers a large area, if blisters are spreading, if you have a fever or the skin turns hot, swollen and weeping in a way that suggests infection, or if it has not settled after about two weeks. The NHS also flags one specific thing after stopping a steroid cream: intense redness, burning, peeling or oozing is a reason to call NHS 111 for advice rather than restarting the cream on your own.

It Was Never the Chlorine — It Was the Hour Afterwards

The pool did not do this to you on its own. The gap between getting out and getting moisturised did. Tonight, before the next swim, do one thing: put a tube of plain emollient in the swim bag, next to the towel, so the decision is already made when you are cold, tired and eyeing the car park. Rinse, pat dry, apply while damp — that sequence is the whole intervention. This article is general health information, not medical advice or a diagnosis; if your skin keeps reacting after every swim, or reacts to things other than pool water, ask a pharmacist or GP about testing rather than cycling through products.
